name: Grace Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a lead driver at a parcel depot on the Northgate estate. We deliver for the big shopping apps, so my van gets loaded at half six and the app gives me about a hundred and forty stops. As lead, I also show new drivers the routes and sort out the mess when the scanner says a parcel is in my van and it isn't. Most days I'm back by four, wrecked from stairs.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm fast and I'm good with people, and the depot manager, Colin, trusts me with the hard routes. I live with my girlfriend Priya, she's a teaching assistant, and we're saving a bit each month for a holiday we keep not taking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thank goodness, and then I'd say that the hype was useful to the bosses anyway. They spent two years telling us the robots were coming so we'd stop asking for raises. I'd say that at the depot and probably on the drivers' forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the job stays hard in the same ways. Stops per day keep creeping up, and every year the app finds a way to add ten more parcels to my van without adding a minute to my day. That's the real pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as lead driver, and I'd finally stand for depot rep with the union, which Colin keeps hinting I should do. I'd keep our savings going at about two hundred a month, and maybe book that holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit tired just thinking about the stop count, but not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the hype was useful to bosses. Can you remember when you noticed that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the pay talks last spring the area manager said we should be grateful for any job with automation coming. Half the drivers took the smaller rise because of that one sentence. I was furious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the stop count do to your body?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My knees, mostly. I'm twenty-seven and I wear a brace on the left one on Fridays. The older drivers say that's how it starts.

say: The **robot hype** helped bosses hold down pay rises at the depot.
With AI calming down, drivers should go back to **asking for raises**.
think: The real pressure is the **stop count** creeping up every year.
Her **knees** are already paying for the pace at twenty-seven.
do: Carry on as **lead driver** on the hard routes at the Northgate depot.
Stand for **union depot rep**, as her manager keeps hinting.
Keep saving about **£200 a month** with her girlfriend.
feel: **Mostly fine**, though worn down by the steady rise in parcels.
S0.quote: every year the app finds a way to add ten more parcels to my van without adding a minute to my day.
fieldNote: She sees AI talk as a **bargaining tool** bosses used against drivers.
Her worry is **physical wear**, a knee brace already, rather than job loss.
She's **trusted by management** yet leans towards the union, and sees no clash.

steps.text: Keep running the hard routes as lead driver at Northgate
Stand for union depot rep at the next election

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say parcel drivers are fine for now, but the people in the depot office aren't. The planners, the customer service team, the people who chase missing parcels. I'd say we should stand with them, because we're next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my driving is safe for a good few years. What changes is the app gets better at squeezing my route, and the office I could have moved into shrinks. I always thought I'd end up in the depot office, and Steady Disruption shuts that door first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try the route tools when other leads have tested them, not before. I'd use the union rep role to push for a rule that AI can't set stop counts without a driver check. And I'd look at the forklift and warehouse supervisor course, as a backup that's still hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for this year, but for the plan I had in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for others to test the tools. Who would you watch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, who runs the Southside route. He tries everything first, then complains for a week, then tells me which bits work. I let him be the guinea pig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sandra on the customer line. She's been there fifteen years and she's the one who actually finds lost parcels. If a chatbot takes her job, nobody will know where anything is.

say: Drivers are fine for now, but **depot office staff** are hit first.
Drivers should **stand with the office**, because hands-on work comes later.
think: Her driving is **safe for years**, but the app squeezes her route harder.
Her hoped-for move into the **depot office** disappears first.
do: Try **route tools** only after other lead drivers have tested them.
Push, as union rep, for a **driver check** on AI-set stop counts.
Look into a **warehouse supervisor** course as a hands-on backup.
feel: **Uneasy**, not about this year but about the future she'd pictured.
S1.quote: I always thought I'd end up in the depot office, and Steady Disruption shuts that door first.
fieldNote: She loses a **career path**, the office job, before she loses her actual job.
Her steady style shows in waiting for a **colleague** to test new tools first.
She worries for an **older office colleague** more than for herself.

steps.text: Use the new route tool once Dev has tested it
Propose a driver check on AI-set stop counts at the depot
Ask about the warehouse supervisor course at the college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a crisis and the government needs to act like it. Proper support for people losing jobs, a say for unions on how robots come in. I'd be posting that, and I'd be at the depot gate talking to every driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd do the maths. The thinking AI in 2028 takes the office and the planning, then the robots around 2031 take the van. By 2031 I'd be thirty-two with bad knees and no qualifications, competing with every other driver for whatever's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the holiday fund and put everything into savings. In the first year I'd start an apprenticeship hunt for something robots struggle with, maybe electrician, because those firms will need people to wire up all the chargers. I'd keep driving while I train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Two years is too fast for the government, never mind for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're not booking anything and we're not moving flat this year. Priya would be calmer than me, because schools need people in the room, so I'd lean on her a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned electrician. Is that a real option for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. My uncle Rafa is an electrician and he's said before he'd ask his firm about taking me on. I always laughed it off, but in this picture I'd ring him that week.

say: AGI by 2028 is a **crisis** that needs real government action.
Unions need a **say** on how robots come into delivery work.
think: Thinking AI takes the **office** in 2028, then robots take the **van** around 2031.
At thirty-two she'd have **bad knees** and no qualifications.
do: Stop the **holiday fund** and move all spare money into savings.
Ring her **uncle**, an electrician, about an apprenticeship at his firm.
Keep **driving** while she trains, to cover the bills.
S2.quote: By 2031 I'd be thirty-two with bad knees and no qualifications, competing with every other driver for whatever's left.
fieldNote: She reads the **three-year gap** clearly: office first, van later.
Her partner's **school job** feels like the household's anchor in this picture.
A family contact makes **electrician** a real route, not a vague hope.

steps.text: Pause the holiday fund and save the full £200 a month
Call Uncle Rafa about an electrician apprenticeship
Rally drivers at the depot gate for union consultation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there are five years to plan, so let's plan. Training budgets, union deals, a clear date when robots start on routes. I'd be saying it calmly at the depot, because panic just helps the bosses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be all right if I start early. The office side goes by 2031, the van side around 2034, so I'd have about seven years of driving. Seven years is enough to finish an apprenticeship, if I start before the robot vans are even on the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask my uncle about the apprenticeship, and if it's a yes, I'd start part-time. I'd use AI now and then to help with the theory, because Priya says it's good for explaining things. And I'd keep pushing for a union training fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but busy. Having a plan helps more than I'd expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to do an apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lead driver bonus, probably, because I'd cut my days. It's about a hundred and twenty a month. Priya and I would cover that from savings for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Colin your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not at first. I'd tell him once I'm sure, because I don't want to lose the good routes while I'm still relying on them.

say: Five years is time to **plan**: training budgets, union deals and clear dates.
Calm is better at the depot, because **panic** only helps the bosses.
think: She'd have about **seven years** of driving before robot vans arrive.
Starting an **apprenticeship early** would put her in a good place.
do: Start a **part-time apprenticeship** with her uncle's firm in the first year.
Use **AI now and then** to help with electrical theory.
Cover the lost **£120 lead bonus** from shared savings.
feel: **Anxious but busy**, with a plan easing the worry.
S3.quote: Seven years is enough to finish an apprenticeship, if I start before the robot vans are even on the road.
fieldNote: She plans to **keep quiet** with her manager until the training is sure.
Her steady approach shows in using AI only as a **study aid**.
Losing the **lead bonus** is a real but manageable cost.

steps.text: Start a part-time electrician apprenticeship with her uncle's firm
Use an AI helper to revise electrical theory
Cover the lost lead bonus from shared savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and final picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. I'd want the union to sign deals now about how the robot vans come in and who gets trained. I'd say it at the depot and at the branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd relax a bit. Ten years plus three for the robots means I'm nearly forty before the van goes. I'd probably still change trade, because of my knees, but on my own timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving as lead for two or three years and save properly. Then I'd do the electrician apprenticeship part-time. And I'd finally book that holiday with Priya, because nobody's robot is coming for my van in the next two summers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a normal way. Like any job that won't last forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your knees would push you to change anyway. Is AI really the reason then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. Maybe it's half and half. The knees say leave by thirty-five, the robots say leave by forty. Either way, the trade is the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell new drivers you train?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Treat this as a job, not a career. Learn the routes, get your pay, but have a second skill by thirty.

say: Ten years is a **gift** if unions use it to sign deals now.
Drivers should know **who gets trained** when robot vans come in.
think: She'd be **nearly forty** before robots take the van.
Her **knees** may push her out before the robots do.
do: Keep driving as **lead** for two or three years and save steadily.
Start the **electrician apprenticeship** part-time after that.
Book the long-delayed **holiday** with her girlfriend.
feel: **Uneasy**, but in a **normal way**, like any job with an end date.
S4.quote: nobody's robot is coming for my van in the next two summers.
fieldNote: When challenged, she admits her **body**, not AI, may set the timing.
She frames delivery as a **job, not a career** for the new drivers she trains.
Ten years lets her **change trade** on her own schedule.

steps.text: Keep driving as lead and save £200 a month
Begin the part-time electrician apprenticeship in year three
Press the union branch for a robot-van training deal

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years before the office goes, five before the van, and I'd be starting from nothing. What would help is a paid apprenticeship scheme for drivers, and the union having a real say on when robots start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about bodies. Everyone talks about robots taking our jobs, but Delivery takes your knees long before any robot takes your van. That should be in your study.

headlineQuote: Delivery takes your knees long before any robot takes your van.
portrait: Grace is a **27-year-old lead driver** at a parcel depot, training new drivers and handling problem routes.
She lives with her girlfriend, a **teaching assistant**, and they save about £200 a month.
She believes bosses used **robot hype** to hold down pay and leans towards union action.
Her backup plan is an **electrician apprenticeship** through her uncle, which she'd start sooner if AGI came fast.
Her mood moves from **uneasy** to **alarmed** in AGI by 2028, and eases with more warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd lose the office route at once and the van soon after.
whatWouldHelp: A real **union say** on when robots start on routes.
